identification.summary: InvisiMole is a cyber-espionage group first reported by ESET in 2018 in connection with targeted operations in Ukraine and Russia; ESET telemetry indicates it has operated since at least 2013 [S1][S2]. Its modular spyware includes two backdoor modules, RC2FM and RC2CL, with capabilities such as webcam and microphone recording, geolocation tracking and collection of recently accessed documents [S2][S3]. The record's Storm-0593 designation could not be verified in this fact-check.
identification.firstObserved: ESET: group active since at least 2013; malware first reported in 2018 [S2][S3].
identification.notes: The Storm-0593 to InvisiMole mapping is unverified (searches found no source linking them). InvisiMole is a separate group from Gamaredon; ESET describes them as distinct actors that cooperate [S3][S4]. CERT-UA tracks the activity as UAC-0035 as reported by SOC Prime [S7].

attribution.confidence: No government attribution of InvisiMole to a specific Russian organization was found in the sources gathered. ESET links InvisiMole operationally to Gamaredon (Russia-linked) but treats them as independent [S3][S4].
attribution.basis: ESET observed InvisiMole tools deployed on systems already compromised by Gamaredon, indicating cooperation between the two groups while ESET treats them as independent [S3][S4].

objectives: Intelligence collection from military and diplomatic organizations and government bodies in Ukraine and Eastern Europe, using spyware that records audio and video, tracks location and collects documents [S3][S4][S7].

targeting.notes: ESET's 2018 report found the malware on a few dozen computers in Ukraine and Russia [S2]. The 2020 activity targeted a few high-profile military and diplomatic organizations in Eastern Europe from late 2019 to at least June 2020 [S3][S4].

capabilities.summary: Modular spyware with a wrapper DLL and two backdoor modules, RC2FM and RC2CL, offering nearly 100 espionage functions, including webcam and microphone access, screenshots and document theft [S2][S3]. The 2020 toolset added a DNS-tunnelling downloader for C2 communication [S3]. Operators gained initial access to targets via Gamaredon's prior compromise: InvisiMole tools were deployed only on systems already infected by Gamaredon [S3][S4]. In March 2022 CERT-UA reported spear-phishing with a ZIP containing an LNK that ran an HTA and VBScript to fetch the LoadEdge backdoor, which then pulled TunnelMode, RC2FM and RC2CL [S7].

campaigns.name: Long-running undetected spyware activity
campaigns.summary: ESET reports the malware went unnoticed until its products found it on compromised machines in Ukraine and Russia; only a few dozen computers were affected and a 2013 compile date remained in the samples.

campaigns.name: ESET public disclosure of InvisiMole
campaigns.summary: ESET published its first analysis of the RC2FM and RC2CL modules; no actor was attributed at that time.

campaigns.name: Military and diplomatic targeting with Gamaredon access
campaigns.summary: ESET reports a refreshed toolset deployed against a few high-profile military and diplomatic organizations in Eastern Europe, only on systems previously compromised by Gamaredon.

campaigns.name: CERT-UA warning on UAC-0035 spear-phishing
campaigns.summary: CERT-UA warned of spear-phishing against Ukrainian state bodies delivering LoadEdge, followed by TunnelMode, RC2FM and RC2CL (reported via SOC Prime secondary coverage).

diamond.adversary: InvisiMole (Storm-0593 designation unverified); cooperates with but is distinct from Gamaredon [S3][S4].
diamond.capability: RC2FM and RC2CL backdoors, DNS-tunnelling downloader, later LoadEdge and TunnelMode [S3][S7].
diamond.infrastructure: Initial access via systems already compromised by Gamaredon [S3][S4]; spear-phishing archives with LNK/HTA/VBScript chain in 2022 [S7]. C2 domains and hosting not captured in the sources gathered.
diamond.victim: Military, diplomatic and government organizations in Ukraine and Eastern Europe [S3][S4][S7].
diamond.socioPolitical: Collection against Ukrainian and regional military and diplomatic entities; the March 2022 campaign followed the start of the full-scale invasion, and a secondary report notes the LoadEdge compile date coincided with 24 February 2022 [S7].
diamond.technology: Windows endpoints; shortcut and script-based delivery; exposure of already-compromised hosts to second-stage tooling [S3][S7].

gaps: The Microsoft Storm-0593 to InvisiMole mapping could not be confirmed by search; claims resting only on it were removed.
The CERT-UA advisory (cert.gov.ua/article/37829) was not opened; 2022 details come from secondary coverage [S7].
No InvisiMole campaign after March 2022 was found in searches; current status unknown.
MITRE ATT&CK group ID for InvisiMole was not confirmed from a source and the record's mitreGroupId remains blank.
Overlap with Gamaredon (a separate group) is cooperation, not merger; the nature of any tasking relationship is unknown.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is Ukrainian and Eastern European military and diplomatic endpoints, particularly hosts already compromised by Gamaredon, plus staff with webcams and microphones [S3][S4]. STEP 2: The adversary relies on a partner's prior access and on spear-phishing, so detecting the first-stage Gamaredon compromise is the main early warning [S3][S7]. STEP 3: Template is initial access (Gamaredon foothold or LNK/HTA/VBScript phishing), then downloader or LoadEdge, then RC2FM/RC2CL spyware with audio, video, location and document collection [S3][S7]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued espionage against Ukrainian and regional military and diplomatic targets. MDCOA is use of the same spyware against allied or coalition personnel and delegations in the region, exploiting their devices' sensors. Candidate indicators: DNS tunnelling traffic from endpoints, LNK files in unsolicited archives launching HTA/VBScript, and Gamaredon-associated infections preceding other implants [S3][S7].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: treat Gamaredon detections as possible precursors to InvisiMole tooling and report them jointly. (2) Authorities: any response on partner networks in Ukraine or the region depends on host-nation and coalition agreements. (3) Mission assurance: devices of deployed personnel and delegations with webcams and microphones are exposed to audio and video collection. (4) Coordination: share indicators with CERT-UA and ESET-style vendor channels through established intelligence-sharing arrangements [S3][S7].
